title: Listening strategies: question types, note-taking and 即時応答
summary: The 50-minute N2 listening section plays each item once. Each of its five question types tells you in advance what to listen for; use that, take minimal notes, and never let a missed item cost you the next one.

sections.heading: Know what each question type gives you before the audio
paragraphs: The listening section is worth a third of the total score and has its own 19-point minimum, so it cannot be neglected. Its five parts differ in when you hear the question and whether the options are printed, and the right tactic follows from that.
bullets: 課題理解 (task-based, about 5 items): the situation and question are read before the conversation, and the options are printed. Listen for what the person will do next or first. The answer is usually the final decision, after earlier suggestions are rejected.

ポイント理解 (point comprehension, about 6 items): the question is read first, then there is a pause to read the printed options, then the audio. Use the pause to read all four options and predict the kind of information you need (a reason, a time, a place).

概要理解 (summary, about 5 items): nothing is printed and the question comes after the audio. Listen for the speaker's main point or purpose, not details. Note the topic and the speaker's overall attitude.
即時応答 (quick response, about 12 items): one short utterance, three spoken replies, nothing printed. Judge which reply is natural. Decide instantly.
統合理解 (integrated, about 4 items): longer conversations, sometimes with two questions on one audio, and the options may be spoken rather than printed. Notes are essential here.

sections.heading: Listen for the decision, not the discussion
paragraphs: N2 dialogues are built around change of mind. A speaker proposes something, the other raises a problem, a second option is considered, and finally one is chosen, often signalled by じゃあ, それなら, やっぱり, そうしよう, or a polite refusal such as 〜はちょっと. The trap options are the things mentioned and abandoned. Train yourself to hold the current candidate lightly and replace it whenever you hear a turning word: でも, ただ, けど, 実は, あ、そうだ. The answer is what stands at the end of the conversation.

Also listen for negatives and exceptions that flip meaning: 〜なくてもいい, 〜以外は, 〜だけは, 〜ないことはない. In 課題理解, the question often asks what to do 最初に or まず; two tasks may be mentioned and only their order distinguishes the right answer.

sections.heading: Note-taking that helps instead of hurts
paragraphs: Writing full words while listening makes you miss the next sentence. Use a symbol system you have practised: a circle for chosen, a cross for rejected, an arrow for change, numbers for times and quantities, and a single kanji or katakana for each key noun. For 課題理解 and ポイント理解, write directly beside the printed options, ticking or crossing as the conversation confirms or eliminates each one. For 統合理解, draw a small table before the audio starts if the introduction tells you there will be several items (four apartments, three plans); then fill each cell with one or two marks as each item is described. The goal is to have the answer visible on the page when the question is read, so that you are not relying on memory.
bullets: Practise a fixed set of symbols until you use them without thinking.
Mark next to the printed options rather than on a separate line.
For integrated items, lay out a grid before the audio begins.
Write numbers and times immediately; they are the easiest to forget.

sections.heading: 即時応答: recognise the function of the utterance
paragraphs: Quick response items go by in about ten seconds each, and there are around twelve of them, so they are a major share of the section. The utterance is usually one of a small set of functions: a request, an offer, an apology, a complaint, a compliment, a report of something that went wrong, an invitation, or a question about the listener's condition. Identify the function, then pick the reply that answers that function naturally. Trap replies reuse a word from the utterance in an unrelated meaning, or answer a different function (thanking someone who apologised, for instance).

The vocabulary here is spoken and often idiomatic: お先に失礼します, 〜てくれない？, 〜ばよかった, 〜んじゃない？, 〜っけ, とんでもない, おかげさまで, まさか. Learn the standard responses to standard phrases. And keep a strict rule: once the next item starts, the previous one is finished. Mark something, anything, and listen. A single missed item is worth one point; letting it distract you through the next two costs three.

sections.heading: Daily habits that transfer to the test
paragraphs: Use the exercise routine on this site every day: listen once without the transcript, answer, check, read the transcript, listen again while reading, shadow each line, then review vocabulary. Shadowing, repeating each line a beat behind the speaker, is the single most effective way to make fast natural speech intelligible, because it forces your ear to segment the sounds you are copying. Increase the playback speed to 1.25× once you can follow at normal speed, so that the real test feels slow. Finally, listen with a purpose during practice: decide what the question type would ask, and check whether you caught it.
bullets: Audio is played once: no rewinding, so prediction and notes replace replay.
The final decision is the answer; abandoned options are distractors.
Identify the function in 即時応答 and answer that function.
